source.title: Sparsity is the enemy of feature extraction (ft. absorption)

record.tranche_reason: The post analytically evaluates absorption and sparsity in a simplified untied SAE on a hierarchical toy dataset, rather than training and measuring real SAEs.
record.gate_note: The post's analytic calculations are its own results. Its Gemma Scope example is attributed to the cited absorption paper, so it is not recorded as a result of this study. Claims about Matryoshka SAEs are presented as a promising approach, not tested results.
record.test_reason: An analytic argument, with no trained SAEs. In a toy orthogonal hierarchy (f2⊂f1), it shows that absorption costs nothing in reconstruction and that the sparsity loss falls as absorption grows. This is a specific argument bearing on V4 (parent latent fails where child takes over) and V6 (the sparsity objective produces the effect). It is T5 rather than T2 because it is a proof sketch, not an empirical method.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also say the post proves the absorption paper's hypothesis that naive sparsity optimization leads to absorption. They argue, without testing, that absorption should occur in all sparsity-based variants (L1, TopK, JumpReLU, crosscoders, transcoders). They suggest Matryoshka SAEs, KL-based and parameter-space methods as possible fixes.
record.recipe_differences: Analytic proof sketch for a simplified untied SAE and orthogonal hierarchical features; no training or empirical measurement of real SAEs.
record.method_sensitivity: The analytic results vary with absorption amount δ and depend on the presence of datapoints with both features (p11>0).
record.problems: The evidence is an analytic argument for a simplified setup with orthogonal features and an assumed hierarchy; it does not empirically test trained SAEs, real models, dictionary size, or alternative objectives.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The real-world Gemma Scope example is attributed to the cited absorption paper rather than reported as this post's own result; the Matryoshka discussion gives no tested outcome.

untested.parts: Dependence on SAE dictionary size. Real SAEs or LLMs. Whether sparsity or λ settings change absorption empirically. The claim that all sparsity-based architectures absorb is argued, not tested.
Splitting itself, as opposed to absorption. Implications for the model's own units. Any test of Matryoshka or other alternative objectives, which the post only proposes as remedies.
Not addressed. The Gemma Scope example is cited from the absorption paper.

missing.what: Reconstruction is perfect for every δ in all three input cases, so absorption has zero reconstruction cost. This is a key premise of the argument.

record.verdict_notes: A short proof sketch with no experiments. The absorption parameterization is imposed, not learned, so R1 and R2 restate the definition. The sparsity formulas mix the norm symbols n and p and assume binary activations, which is inconsistent with the derived z values. Only the sign of the effect is robust. The Gemma Scope example and the transcoder absorption claim are cited results and are correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: No dictionary-size sweep or test of coarse features being replaced by finer features.
No large-model or open-release SAE results.
No test of nested feature families or their geometric closeness.
The post analyzes parent-latent failure under absorption in a toy hierarchy, but does not vary SAE size or test whether changing sparsity settings fixes the failure.
No comparison of larger- and smaller-dictionary latents or test for novel latents.
The post analytically studies an Lp sparsity penalty, but does not train or compare SAEs with alternative objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs.

rows.subject: simplified untied SAE
rows.baseline: For input f1 alone, z1=1 and z2=0; at δ=0 with input f1+f2, z1=1 and z2=1
rows.value: For input f1+f2, z1=0 and z2=1
rows.locator: Reconstruction under δ-absorption, Case 2; Sparsity under δ-absorption, Case 2
rows.note: At full absorption the parent latent does not fire on the parent-plus-child input, while the child latent does.
rows.check: Holds by construction. δ-absorption is defined via e1=f1−δf2, so z1=0 at δ=1 is assumed, not derived. The row shows what absorption looks like, not that it arises.

rows.subject: simplified untied SAE
rows.operation_detail: Calculate encoder activations under arbitrary δ-absorption
rows.note: The parent latent's activation on the combined input decreases with δ and reaches zero at δ=1.
rows.check: Also by construction from the encoder parameterization. At intermediate δ the parent's activation is reduced, not eliminated.

source_check.problem: none; z1=1−δ follows from the defined encoder e1=f1−δf2.

rows.subject: simplified untied SAE
rows.operation_detail: Calculate Lp sparsity loss at zero absorption
rows.note: Analytic expression for the loss at no absorption.
rows.check: This is the δ=0 reference expression, a baseline rather than an effect. It should be folded into the baselines of R4–R5. Its exponent uses n while Case 3 uses p, which is a notational inconsistency.

rows.subject: simplified untied SAE
rows.operation_detail: Calculate Lp sparsity loss at full absorption
rows.note: The post states that this loss is lower than at δ=0 when p11>0.
rows.check: The expression assumes binary encoder activations (fenc∈{0,1}). It is not consistent with the derived z1=1−δ, z2=1, whose Lp sum would be (1−δ)^p+1. The derivation is loose.

source_check.problem: The text writes the δ=0 exponent as 1/n (n-norm), which is the same norm order the post later calls p. The binary-activation assumption is stated for Case 1. The endpoint values match a root-norm of 0/1 activations but not the post's own Lsp=E[Σ|z|^p].

rows.subject: simplified untied SAE
rows.operation_detail: Calculate Lp sparsity loss for arbitrary δ
rows.note: The loss expression decreases as δ increases for p11>0, as stated in the post.
rows.check: The (2−δ)^(1/p) form does not follow from the stated activations z1=1−δ, z2=1. The direction (loss falls with δ) holds, but the formula is heuristic.

source_check.problem: none beyond the known looseness: the (2−δ)^(1/p) form is asserted, not derived from z1=1−δ, z2=1.

rows.subject: simplified untied SAE
rows.operation_detail: Differentiate sparsity loss with respect to absorption
rows.value: −p11/p⋅(2−δ)^(1/p−1), stated to be negative when p11>0
rows.note: The analytic derivative indicates that minimizing the stated sparsity loss favors increasing absorption.
rows.check: This also bears on V4: for any p and p11>0, the sparsity penalty favors absorption, which supports the claim that sparsity tuning does not remove it. It inherits the derivation looseness of R5.

source_check.problem: Fraction layout is garbled, but the text matches −(p11/p)(2−δ)^(1/p−1), the derivative of the Case 3 formula. The post switches to Lsp=E|z|^p there, which differs from Case 3.

relationships.reason: The parent latent drops out on parent+child inputs under absorption (R1, R2, which are by construction). Reconstruction is unaffected at any δ and sparsity loss strictly decreases with δ, so the objective drives absorption (R6; missing reconstruction row).

relation.reason: It gives an analytic argument that bears directly on V4 and V6, though it has no empirical test.

tranche.reason: The post is a specific analytic argument (a proof sketch) that sparsity-trained SAEs absorb hierarchical parents. It argues that the clean hierarchical-splitting picture needs restating, and it supports the challenge versions V4 and V6. T5 explicitly covers 'a specific argument'. T2 would fit only if the absorption question counted as the original's question.

source_check.notes: The post is a proof sketch with no experiments. Absorption is built into the encoder definition, and (2−δ)^(1/p) does not follow from z1=1−δ, z2=1. Lsp is defined three different ways: on ^h, as an n-norm, and as E|z|^p. The text has a TODO. Claims about TopK, JumpReLU, crosscoders and Matryoshka are untested expectations.

statements.problem: none. For this study the text gives a simplified untied bias-free SAE on orthogonal hierarchical features, perfect reconstruction at any δ, a negative derivative when p11>0, and z1=1−δ by construction. Note that SAE size is never varied.
